chapter: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
title: Kickbacks to club owners
summary: Musicians gave back part of scale; Luis Russell was fined and Otis Johnson refused to kick back.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: The white representatives wouldn't come up - or did they have white representatives to come up to the Apollo and the Savoy at the time?
They didn't do nothing but kick back.
What do you mean by kick back?
You were supposed to get so much. Like if you had a job playing in a theatre you were supposed to get $100 a week. They gave you $100 and said, but you got to give us back $25.
No, that's the way they did then.
I mean, you would have to give it back to the band-leader? The owner of the club? You had to give the money back to the club owner?
Give it back to the club owner.
So in other words the club owner was reporting that you were making the scale but the fact was -

They would pay you the scale and you'd give the scale to the union. The union would give you your money and you'd take that $25 or $30 and give it back to the man that owned the place. But they caught up with Louis Russell and put a fine on him. Otis Johnson, trumpet player, said, "I'm not going to give back nothing. I played for that and I'm keeping it." So we had a trial board and they didn't fine Russell or nothing like that. They just called him the black sheep of the family... He apologized in a hurry too. Otis Johnson didn't give back no money but two-thirds of the musicians in New York working then, they kicked back, what we called it.
Yeah, the kickback, right. Was that even the practice at the Apollo and the Savoy?
Anywhere. No, not Savoy and not the Saratoga Club.
